analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the federal estate tax drew 79 cosponsors, all Republicans, but never advanced past a referral to the House Ways and Means Committee and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely, starting the day it was signed into law. The estate tax only applies to the largest inheritances in the country; families pay nothing unless an estate is worth millions of dollars. Repeal would mean heirs to those fortunes owe no federal tax on what they receive, and the money the tax raises would have to come from somewhere else or be added to the deficit. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates — families whose taxable estates exceed the multi-million-dollar exemption — would pay nothing on their inheritance. Wealth-management and trust firms that serve those families would also benefit from clients keeping more of their wealth.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and transfers after enactment. [S3]
Because the tax applies only to estates above a large exemption, the direct benefit goes to the heirs of the biggest estates, who would owe no federal tax on inheritances worth millions. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and therefore all other taxpayers, loses the tens of billions of dollars a year the estate tax raises. Either other taxes go up or deficits grow to cover the gap.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes the only federal tax on large accumulated wealth passed between generations, which is also the tax that limits the growth of dynastic fortunes; the forgone revenue must be replaced by other taxes, more borrowing, or cuts elsewhere. [S3]

An honest supporter must acknowledge that repeal mainly helps a small group: without an exemption, no estate under millions of dollars owes any estate tax, so ordinary families are unaffected except through the budget effect of the lost revenue. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain is concentrated and large for heirs of the biggest fortunes, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across everyone who pays federal taxes or who would be affected by deficit spending. The bill does not pair the tax cut with any replacement revenue, so the public cost is real and open-ended.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; no vote ever happened in either chamber.

narrative.text: Representative Mac Thornberry introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act on January 6, 2015, the first day of the new Congress, with 22 original cosponsors. [S1]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction. [S1]

That referral was the only action the bill ever received; 79 members, all Republicans, cosponsored it, but the Ways and Means Committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and neither the House nor the Senate ever considered the bill. [S4][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The tax repeal did not happen, so the federal estate tax remained in place on the largest estates. Large fortunes and their heirs were not relieved of the tax; a narrow group of wealthy families lost the chance at a large tax cut, while the general public was spared the cost of replacing that revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal estate tax survived; repeal failed

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member (not the committee)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 114th Congress and recruited 22 original cosponsors. [S1]

for.name: 79 of 247 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the estate tax repeal; every cosponsor was a Republican. [S4]

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 6, 2015 and never took it up; no markup, vote, or report followed, so the bill died in committee when the Congress ended. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: All 79 cosponsors were House Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no roll call ever occurred because the bill never left committee. [S4][S5]

industries.industry: Heirs to very large estates and wealthy families
industries.note: Repeal would remove the federal tax on inheritances of many millions of dollars — the bill's main beneficiary group. Their gain comes directly out of federal revenue, which other taxpayers must cover.

industries.industry: Estate planning and private wealth management
industries.note: Clients would keep more wealth and have more money to invest, but the estate tax itself drives much of the demand for trust and estate planning services, which repeal would shrink. The net effect on the industry is genuinely two-sided.
